# Answer key - Chapter 12: Incident response, BCM, risk and compliance {.unnumbered}

<!-- Source-only: this directory is excluded from the render in _quarto.yml
     ("!answers/"). Never link these files from a chapter. Numbering must
     match the chapter's Self-check section 1:1. -->

**Q1** *(tests @sec-12-events-incidents-breaches · basic)* - **Correct: b.**
@def-incident states it verbatim: all incidents are events; not all events
are incidents; and only some incidents become breaches. Option d describes
an event, not a breach.

**Q2** *(tests @sec-12-ir-lifecycle · basic)* - **Correct: c.**
@def-irlifecycle gives the order Preparation; Detection & Analysis;
Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Post-Incident Analysis. Option d mixes
in NIST CSF-style function names that are not the SP 800-61 phases.

**Q3** *(tests @sec-12-ir-lifecycle · basic)* - **Accepted answers:**
"a blocked user may still hold a valid session token", "federated identity
separates authentication from authorisation, so the relying party must act
too" (any phrasing that says federated identity separates authentication
from authorisation, so a blocked user may still hold a valid session token
and containment may require actions on both the identity provider and the
relying party).

**Q4** *(tests @sec-12-business-continuity · basic)* - **Correct: b.**
The RPO states how much recent data the organisation can afford to lose;
the RTO (option a) states how quickly the service must be back. Risk
appetite and blast radius are concepts from other parts of the course.

**Q5** *(tests @sec-12-risk-audit-compliance · basic)* - **Accepted answers:**
"the customer inherits the provider's control set for the infrastructure
layer, but the compliance of what the customer builds on top remains the
customer's own task", "inheriting the provider's compliance for its layers
while remaining responsible for your own software" (any phrasing with both
halves: inheritance for the provider-operated layer, continued own
responsibility for what is built on top).

**Q6** *(tests @sec-12-risk-audit-compliance · basic)* - **Correct: b.**
Comer (2021, p. 242): side channels and back doors are structural risks
stopped by neither a firewall nor a password, so they are exactly the risks
a register exists to record and to accept knowingly.

**Q7 - applied scenario** *(tests @sec-12-ir-lifecycle · applied)* -
**Model answer:** Containment: disable the account *and* revoke its
sessions (federated identity means a valid token may outlive the block),
and isolate the affected workload; IAM and the management plane are the top
priorities (Session 7). Eradication: rotate *all* credentials, not just one
password, enforce MFA and additional policy conditions (Session 7); delete
the tampered image and any old images, function code and IaC the attacker
may have altered, because a careless redeployment could let the attacker
back in (Session 5's immutable pattern makes replacement simpler than
expulsion). Recovery: redeploy hardened versions from IaC after analysing
images, resources and templates for remaining backdoors, and restore data
from the clean, tested backup (Session 11); capture incident data under
chain of custody (Session 10). What the plan misses: patching the running
container leaves any backdoor in the image and its redeployments;
re-enabling the account with only a new password ignores other stolen
credentials, live session tokens and missing MFA; and closing without
Post-Incident Analysis loses the lessons that must feed back into
preparation. Grading notes: full credit requires the three phases in order,
at least the token/rotation point and the delete-and-rebuild point, and an
earlier-session control named per step; partial credit for a correct
critique without the phase structure.

## Sketch answers to the chapter exercises

(1) *(@exr-12-event-incident-breach)* An event is any observable occurrence;
an incident is an event that violates policy or threatens CIA and demands a
response; a breach is a successful compromise leading to unauthorised data
access or extraction. A breach may trigger legal or regulatory notification.

(2) *(@exr-12-four-phases)* Preparation (baseline, monitoring, tested
backups); Detection & Analysis (trustworthy off-host logs for the timeline);
Containment/Eradication/Recovery (MFA and IAM from Session 7, immutable
images from Session 5, backups from Session 11); Post-Incident Analysis
(feeds lessons back into preparation).

(3) *(@exr-12-rebuild-vs-patch)* Because the attacker may hold stolen
credentials and may have left back doors in images, serverless code or IaC;
rotating credentials revokes their access, and rebuilding from clean
definitions removes hidden footholds a patch would leave in place.

(4) *(@exr-12-rto-rpo)* RTO is how quickly a service must be restored; RPO
is how much recent data may be lost. RPO sets backup frequency (lose at most
that much); RTO sets the required restore speed and the recovery design.

(5) *(@exr-12-register-inheritance)* A risk register lists identified risks,
their severity and mitigation actions, aligning effort with risk appetite.
Compliance inheritance means inheriting the provider's control set for the
layers it operates while remaining responsible for the compliance of one's
own software: the shared-responsibility model expressed in the language of
audit.
